where the external states (drawn with curly lines for concreteness) can be either spin-0 or spin-1, and the internal electronic states I,I′I,I^{\prime} are summed over. Using the in-medium Feynman rules (see e.g. Ref. [93]) we obtain, for the first diagram:

−i​Π𝒪1,𝒪2=(−1)V​∑I′​I∫−∞∞d​ε2​π​tr(⟨I′|𝒪1ei​𝒒⋅𝒙|I⟩⟨I|𝒪2e−i𝒒⋅𝒙|I′⟩)(ε+ω−εI′+i​δI′)​(ε−εI+i​δI),-i\,\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}}=\frac{(-1)}{V}\sum_{I^{\prime}I}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\varepsilon}{2\pi}\,\frac{\text{tr}\left(\langle I^{\prime}|\,\mathcal{O}_{1}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|I\rangle\langle I|\,\mathcal{O}_{2}\,e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|I^{\prime}\rangle\right)}{(\varepsilon+\omega-\varepsilon_{I^{\prime}}+i\delta_{I^{\prime}})(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{I}+i\delta_{I})}\,, (75)

where VV is the total volume, “tr” represents the spin trace, and δI(′)≡δsgn(εI(′)−εF)\delta_{I^{(\prime)}}\equiv\delta\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon_{I^{(\prime)}}-\varepsilon_{F}) with δ→0+\delta\to 0^{+}. Note that the i​δi\delta prescription for electron propagators is different from the vacuum theory, and depends on whether the state is above or below the Fermi energy εF\varepsilon_{F}; using the correct i​δi\delta prescription is crucial for ensuring causality. Meanwhile, the matrix elements coming from the vertices are

⟨I′|𝒪1​ei​𝒒⋅𝒙|I⟩=∫d3​x​[ΨI′∗​(𝒙)​𝒪1​ΨI​(𝒙)]​ei​𝒒⋅𝒙,\langle I^{\prime}|\,\mathcal{O}_{1}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|I\rangle=\int d^{3}x\,\bigl[\Psi_{I^{\prime}}^{*}(\bm{x})\,\mathcal{O}_{1}\Psi_{I}(\bm{x})\bigr]\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}\,, (76)

and likewise for ⟨I|𝒪2e−i𝒒⋅𝒙|I′⟩\langle I|\,\mathcal{O}_{2}\,e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|I^{\prime}\rangle. Here 𝒪1,2\mathcal{O}_{1,2} are matrices in spin space, and may involve spatial derivatives acting on the electronic wave functions. For example, for the velocity operator defined in Eq. (27) (which is proportional to the identity matrix in spin space), we have

⟨I′|vjei​𝒒⋅𝒙|I⟩=−i2​me⟨I′|∇↔jei​𝒒⋅𝒙|I⟩=−i2​me∫d3x[ΨI′∗(∇jΨI)−(∇jΨI′∗)ΨI]ei​𝒒⋅𝒙.\big\langle I^{\prime}\big|\,v^{j}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}\,\big|I\big\rangle=-\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\,\big\langle I^{\prime}\big|\,\overleftrightarrow{\nabla}_{\hskip-2.0ptj}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}\,\big|I\big\rangle=-\frac{i}{2m_{e}}\int d^{3}x\,\bigl[\Psi_{I^{\prime}}^{*}\,(\nabla_{j}\Psi_{I})-(\nabla_{j}\Psi_{I^{\prime}}^{*})\,\Psi_{I}\bigr]\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}\,. (77)

We can evaluate the energy integral in Eq. (75) by examining the pole structure of the integrand in the complex plane. If δI′\delta_{I^{\prime}} and δI\delta_{I} have the same sign (i.e. if both I′I^{\prime} and II are above or below the Fermi energy), the two poles are on the same side of the real axis and they have opposite residues; the integral therefore vanishes upon closing the contour via either +i​∞+i\infty or −i​∞-i\infty. So we must have one state above the Fermi energy and one below it, in which case there is one pole on each side of the real axis; closing the contour via either +i​∞+i\infty or −i​∞-i\infty to pick up the residue at one of the poles, we obtain

∫−∞∞d​ε2​π​1(ε+ω−εI′+i​δI′)​(ε−εI+i​δI)={iω−ωI′​I+i​δif δI′>0, δI<0;−iω−ωI′​I−i​δif δI′<0, δI>0.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\varepsilon}{2\pi}\,\frac{1}{(\varepsilon+\omega-\varepsilon_{I^{\prime}}+i\delta_{I^{\prime}})(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{I}+i\delta_{I})}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{i}{\omega-\omega_{I^{\prime}I}+i\delta}&\text{if \, $\delta_{I^{\prime}}>0$, $\delta_{I}<0$}\,;\\[12.0pt] -\dfrac{i}{\omega-\omega_{I^{\prime}I}-i\delta}&\text{if \, $\delta_{I^{\prime}}<0$, $\delta_{I}>0$}\,.\end{cases} (78)

Here ωI′​I≡εI′−εI\omega_{I^{\prime}I}\equiv\varepsilon_{I^{\prime}}-\varepsilon_{I}, and δ→0+\delta\to 0^{+}. All cases discussed above can be concisely summarized as:

∫−∞∞d​ε2​π​1(ε+ω−εI′+i​δI′)​(ε−εI+i​δI)=−i⁡(fI′−fI)ω−ωI′​I+i​δI′​I,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\varepsilon}{2\pi}\,\frac{1}{(\varepsilon+\omega-\varepsilon_{I^{\prime}}+i\delta_{I^{\prime}})(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{I}+i\delta_{I})}=\frac{-i\,(f_{I^{\prime}}-f_{I})}{\omega-\omega_{I^{\prime}I}+i\delta_{I^{\prime}I}}\,, (79)

where fIf_{I}, fI′f_{I^{\prime}} are the occupation numbers (equal to 1 for states below the Fermi energy, 0 for states above it), and δI′​I≡δ​sgn​(ωI′​I)\delta_{I^{\prime}I}\equiv\delta\,\text{sgn}(\omega_{I^{\prime}I}). We therefore obtain

Π𝒪1,𝒪2=−1V∑I′​IfI′−fIω−ωI′​I+i​δI′​Itr(⟨I′|𝒪1ei​𝒒⋅𝒙|I⟩⟨I|𝒪2e−i𝒒⋅𝒙|I′⟩).\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}}=-\frac{1}{V}\,\sum_{I^{\prime}I}\,\frac{f_{I^{\prime}}-f_{I}}{\omega-\omega_{I^{\prime}I}+i\delta_{I^{\prime}I}}\,\text{tr}\Bigl(\langle I^{\prime}|\,\mathcal{O}_{1}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|I\rangle\langle I|\,\mathcal{O}_{2}\,e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|I^{\prime}\rangle\Bigr)\,. (80)

As the simplest example, setting 𝒪1=𝒪2=𝟙\mathcal{O}_{1}=\mathcal{O}_{2}=\mathbb{1} in Eq. (80), we obtain Π𝟙,𝟙\Pi_{\mathbb{1},\mathbb{1}}, and hence the dielectric via Eq. (36), which reproduces the familiar Lindhard formula (see e.g. Ref. [98] and recent discussions in Refs. [58, 59]).

Now move on to the second diagram in Eq. (74). While we have shown in Sec. III that contributions to absorption rates from this diagram can be eliminated using the Ward identity, we present its result here for completeness and also to allow for an explicit check of the Ward identity. In this diagram, the electron propagator starts and ends at the same time point and time-ordering becomes ambiguous. The correct prescription is to take the normal-ordered product of creation and annihilation operators, and the loop is simply proportional to the electron number operator [93]. Again writing the result in terms of occupation number fIf_{I}, we find

Π𝒪′=−1V∑IfItr⟨I|𝒪|I⟩.\Pi^{\prime}_{\mathcal{O}}=-\frac{1}{V}\,\sum_{I}\,f_{I}\,\text{tr}\langle I|\,\mathcal{O}|I\rangle\,. (81)

Note that Π𝒪′\Pi^{\prime}_{\mathcal{O}} is purely real at all orders. With Eqs. (80) and (81) one can readily verify the relations implied by the Ward identity, Eqs. (29) and (53).

A.2 Real Part of the One-loop Self-energy in a Metal

We now apply Eq. (80) to the case of a metal. As discussed in Sec. V, we model the electrons near the Fermi surface of a metal as free quasiparticles with an effective mass m∗m_{*} and energy eigenstates labeled by momentum. The sum over I,I′I,I^{\prime} becomes integrals over 𝒌,𝒌′\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}, and we have

Π𝒪1,𝒪2=ReΠ𝒪1,𝒪2=−1V∫V​d3​k′(2​π)3∫V​d3​k(2​π)3f𝒌′−f𝒌ω−k′22​m∗+k22​m∗tr(⟨𝒌′|𝒪1ei​𝒒⋅𝒙|𝒌⟩⟨𝒌|𝒪2e−i𝒒⋅𝒙|𝒌′⟩).\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}}=\text{Re}\,\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}}=-\frac{1}{V}\int\frac{V\,d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int\frac{V\,d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{f_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}-f_{\bm{k}}}{\omega-\frac{k^{\prime 2}}{2m_{*}}+\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}}\,\text{tr}\Bigl(\langle\bm{k}^{\prime}|\,\mathcal{O}_{1}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|\bm{k}\rangle\langle\bm{k}|\,\mathcal{O}_{2}\,e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|\bm{k}^{\prime}\rangle\Bigr)\,. (82)

Note that the i​δi\delta in the denominator is irrelevant since the intermediate states cannot go on-shell and Π𝒪1,𝒪2\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}} is real at one-loop level.

Let us first consider Π𝟙,𝟙\Pi_{\mathbb{1},\mathbb{1}}. For the matrix element part, we have

⟨𝒌′| 1​ei​𝒒⋅𝒙|𝒌⟩=\displaystyle\langle\bm{k}^{\prime}|\,\mathbb{1}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|\bm{k}\rangle= 1V​∫d3​x​ei⁡(𝒌+𝒒−𝒌′)⋅𝒙​ 1=(2​π)3V​δ3​(𝒌+𝒒−𝒌′)​ 1,\displaystyle\;\frac{1}{V}\int d^{3}x\,e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\cdot\bm{x}}\,\mathbb{1}=\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{V}\,\delta^{3}(\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\,\mathbb{1}\,, (83)
tr(⟨𝒌′| 1ei​𝒒⋅𝒙|𝒌⟩⟨𝒌| 1e−i𝒒⋅𝒙|𝒌′⟩)=\displaystyle\text{tr}\Bigl(\langle\bm{k}^{\prime}|\,\mathbb{1}\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|\bm{k}\rangle\langle\bm{k}|\,\mathbb{1}\,e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{x}}|\bm{k}^{\prime}\rangle\Bigr)=  2​(2​π)3V​δ3​(𝒌+𝒒−𝒌′)​1V​∫d3​x=2​(2​π)3V​δ3​(𝒌+𝒒−𝒌′).\displaystyle\;2\,\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{V}\,\delta^{3}(\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\,\frac{1}{V}\int d^{3}x=2\,\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{V}\,\delta^{3}(\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\,. (84)

Therefore,

Π𝟙,𝟙=−2∫d3​k(2​π)3f𝒌+𝒒−f𝒌ω−(𝒌+𝒒)22​m∗+k22​m∗=−2∫d3​k(2​π)3f𝒌+𝒒−f𝒌ω−𝒌⋅𝒒m∗−q22​m∗.\Pi_{\mathbb{1},\mathbb{1}}=-2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,\frac{f_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}-f_{\bm{k}}}{\omega-\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q})^{2}}{2m_{*}}+\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}}=-2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,\frac{f_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}-f_{\bm{k}}}{\omega-\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{m_{*}}-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{*}}}\,. (85)

Expanding in small qq and integrating by parts, we find

Π𝟙,𝟙=\displaystyle\Pi_{\mathbb{1},\mathbb{1}}= −2∫d3​k(2​π)3(𝒒⋅∇f𝒌+…)(1ω+𝒌⋅𝒒m∗​ω2+…)\displaystyle\;-2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\left(\bm{q}\cdot\nabla f_{\bm{k}}+\dots\right)\left(\frac{1}{\omega}+\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{m_{*}\omega^{2}}+\dots\right)
=\displaystyle=  2∫d3​k(2​π)3f𝒌(𝒒⋅∇+…)(1ω+𝒌⋅𝒒m∗​ω2+…)\displaystyle\;2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,f_{\bm{k}}\left(\bm{q}\cdot\nabla+\dots\right)\left(\frac{1}{\omega}+\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{m_{*}\omega^{2}}+\dots\right)
≃\displaystyle\simeq  2​∫d3​k(2​π)3​f𝒌​q2m∗​ω2=q2ω2​nem∗,\displaystyle\;2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,f_{\bm{k}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{m_{*}\omega^{2}}\,=\,\frac{q^{2}}{\omega^{2}}\,\frac{n_{e}}{m_{*}}\,, (86)

=\displaystyle=  2∫d3​k(2​π)3f𝒌(𝒒⋅∇−12qiqj∇i∇j+…)(1ω+𝒌⋅𝒒m∗​ω2+…)(k22​me2+𝒌⋅𝒒2​me2+…)\displaystyle\;2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,f_{\bm{k}}\left(\bm{q}\cdot\nabla-\frac{1}{2}\,q^{i}q^{j}\,\nabla_{i}\nabla_{j}+\dots\right)\left(\frac{1}{\omega}+\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{m_{*}\omega^{2}}+\dots\right)\left(\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{e}^{2}}+\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{2m_{e}^{2}}+\dots\right)
≃\displaystyle\simeq  2​∫d3​k(2​π)3​f𝒌​k2​q2+2​(𝒌⋅𝒒)22​me2​m∗​ω2=kF22​me2​q2ω2​nem∗,\displaystyle\;2\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,f_{\bm{k}}\,\frac{k^{2}q^{2}+2(\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q})^{2}}{2m_{e}^{2}m_{*}\omega^{2}}\,=\,\frac{k_{F}^{2}}{2m_{e}^{2}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{\omega^{2}}\,\frac{n_{e}}{m_{*}}\,, (87)

where we have used f𝒌=Θ⁡(kF−k)f_{\bm{k}}=\Theta(k_{F}-k), and ne=2(2​π)3​43​π​kF3n_{e}=\frac{2}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{4}{3}\pi k_{F}^{3}. Finally, since Eq. (87) is invariant under (ω,𝒒)→(−ω,−𝒒)(\omega,\bm{q})\to(-\omega,-\bm{q}), we have Π𝟙,v¯2​(Q)=Πv¯2,𝟙​(−Q)=Πv¯2,𝟙​(Q)\Pi_{\mathbb{1},\bar{v}^{2}}(Q)=\Pi_{\bar{v}^{2},\mathbb{1}}(-Q)=\Pi_{\bar{v}^{2},\mathbb{1}}(Q).

A.3 Imaginary Part of the Two-loop Self-energy in a Metal

The one-loop self-energies calculated above are purely real: both electrons cannot go on-shell if their energies and momenta differ by Qμ=(ω,𝒒)Q^{\mu}=(\omega,\bm{q}) with ω≫q\omega\gg q. The leading contribution to Im​Π𝒪1,𝒪2​(Q)\text{Im}\,\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}}(Q) comes from two-loop diagrams with an internal phonon line. In this section, we compute them first in the case of a normal conductor, and then discuss the corrections needed in the superconductor case when ω\omega approaches the gap 2​Δ2\Delta.

Cut diagrams.

Here each propagator is labeled by a four-momentum that consists of the energy it carries and the momentum label of the electron or phonon state. In each diagram, we denote four-momentum flowing into the 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} vertex from the electron propagator as Kμ=(ε,𝒌)K^{\mu}=(\varepsilon,\bm{k}), and the phonon four-momentum (with direction indicated by the arrow) as Q′μ=(ω′,𝒒′)Q^{\prime\mu}=(\omega^{\prime},\bm{q}^{\prime}). The electron and phonon propagators are denoted by i​GiG and i​GphiG^{\text{ph}}, respectively, with

GK=1ε−k22​m∗+i​δε,GQ′ph=1ω′−ωq′+i​δ−1ω′+ωq′−i​δ=2​ωq′ω′2−ωq′2+i​δ,G_{K}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon-\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}+i\delta_{\varepsilon}}\,,\qquad G_{Q^{\prime}}^{\text{ph}}=\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}-\omega_{q^{\prime}}+i\delta}-\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}+\omega_{q^{\prime}}-i\delta}=\frac{2\,\omega_{q^{\prime}}}{\omega^{\prime 2}-\omega_{q^{\prime}}^{2}+i\delta}\,, (91)

where δε=δ​sgn​(ε−εF)\delta_{\varepsilon}=\delta\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{F}), δ→0+\delta\to 0^{+}, and ωq′=cs​q′\omega_{q^{\prime}}=c_{s}q^{\prime}. The electron-phonon vertex yq′=Ce-ph​q′2​ωq′​ρTy_{q^{\prime}}=\frac{C_{\text{e-ph}}q^{\prime}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{q^{\prime}}\rho_{T}}}, while the vertices associated with operator insertions 𝒪1,2\mathcal{O}_{1,2} yield the momentum space representations of these operators, 𝒪~1,2\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{1,2}, whose arguments are the incoming and outgoing electrons’ four-momenta. We have assumed exact momentum conservation and neglected Umklapp processes; the latter may introduce an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) correction to the final results which is more difficult to calculate.

By the optical theorem, 2​Im​Π𝒪1,𝒪22\,\text{Im}\,\Pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2}} is given by the sum of cut diagrams. For the first diagram, Eq. (88), there is only one possible cut to put all intermediate states on-shell, i.e. the one through the phonon propagator and the two electron propagators carrying momenta KK and K+Q−Q′K+Q-Q^{\prime}. By the cutting rules, we should replace

GQ′ph→\displaystyle G_{Q^{\prime}}^{\text{ph}}\to −2​π​i​[δ⁡(ω′−ωq′)+δ⁡(ω′+ωq′)],\displaystyle\;-2\pi i\bigl[\delta(\omega^{\prime}-\omega_{q^{\prime}})+\delta(\omega^{\prime}+\omega_{q^{\prime}})\bigr]\,, (92)
GK→\displaystyle G_{K}\to −2​π​i​sgn​(ε−εF)​δ​(ε−k22​m∗),\displaystyle\;-2\pi i\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{F})\,\delta\biggl(\varepsilon-\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}\biggr)\,, (93)
GK+Q−Q′→\displaystyle G_{K+Q-Q^{\prime}}\to −2​π​i​sgn​(ε+ω−ω′−εF)​δ​(ε+ω−ω′−(𝒌+𝒒−𝒒′)22​m∗).\displaystyle\;-2\pi i\,\text{sgn}(\varepsilon+\omega-\omega^{\prime}-\varepsilon_{F})\,\delta\biggl(\varepsilon+\omega-\omega^{\prime}-\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{q}^{\prime})^{2}}{2m_{*}}\biggr)\,. (94)

For ω>0\omega>0, the on-shell condition requires ω′>0\omega^{\prime}>0, ε<εF\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{F} and ε+ω−ω′>εF\varepsilon+\omega-\omega^{\prime}>\varepsilon_{F}; this corresponds to a process where an electron jumps out of the Fermi sphere by absorbing Qμ=(ω,𝒒)Q^{\mu}=(\omega,\bm{q}) while emitting a phonon to conserve momentum. =\displaystyle= −∫d3​k(2​π)3∫d3​q′(2​π)3 2πδ(ω+k22​m∗−(𝒌+𝒒−𝒒′)22​m∗−ωq′)f𝒌(1−f𝒌+𝒒−𝒒′)yq′2\displaystyle\;-\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int\frac{d^{3}q^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,2\pi\,\delta\biggl(\omega+\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}-\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{q}^{\prime})^{2}}{2m_{*}}-\omega_{q^{\prime}}\biggr)\,f_{\bm{k}}\,\bigl(1-f_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{q}^{\prime}}\bigr)\,y_{q^{\prime}}^{2}
GK−Q′2​tr​[𝒪~1​(K−Q′,K+Q−Q′)​𝒪~2​(K+Q−Q′,K−Q′)],\displaystyle\hskip 55.0ptG_{K-Q^{\prime}}^{2}\,\text{tr}\Bigl[\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{1}(K-Q^{\prime},K+Q-Q^{\prime})\,\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{2}(K+Q-Q^{\prime},K-Q^{\prime})\Bigr]\,, (96)

where we have shifted the integration variable 𝒌→𝒌−𝒒′\bm{k}\to\bm{k}-\bm{q}^{\prime} to arrive at the last line.

Small qq expansion.

As in the previous section, we expand the integrand in small qq. The electron propagators become:

GK+Q=\displaystyle G_{K+Q}= 1k22​m∗+ω−(𝒌+𝒒)22​m∗=1ω−𝒌⋅𝒒m∗−q22​m∗=1ω+𝒌⋅𝒒m∗​ω2+…,\displaystyle\;\frac{1}{\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}+\omega-\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q})^{2}}{2m_{*}}}=\frac{1}{\omega-\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{m_{*}}-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{*}}}=\frac{1}{\omega}+\frac{\bm{k}\cdot\bm{q}}{m_{*}\omega^{2}}+\dots\,, (99)

Including the gap.

We have presented the calculation of cut diagrams assuming a normal metal for simplicity. Accounting for pairing of electrons in the BCS theory introduces a slight modification in the final result in the form of a coherence factor [94]. Concretely, for the imaginary part of two-loop self-energies computed above, this amounts to replacing

in Eq. (102), where we have abbreviated 𝒌+𝒒−𝒒′≡𝒌′\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\bm{q}^{\prime}\equiv\bm{k}^{\prime} and defined ϵk≡k22​m∗−εF\epsilon_{k}\equiv\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{*}}-\varepsilon_{F}, Ek≡ϵk2+Δ2E_{k}\equiv\sqrt{\epsilon_{k}^{2}+\Delta^{2}} (and similarly for ϵk′\epsilon_{k^{\prime}}, Ek′E_{k^{\prime}}). The energy of the electron-hole pair is therefore constrained to be Ek+Ek′≥2​ΔE_{k}+E_{k^{\prime}}\geq 2\Delta.

Appendix B Absorption in Anisotropic Targets

Since the benchmark materials considered in this work (Si, Ge and Al-SC) are near-isotropic, in the main text of the paper we worked under the simplifying assumption that the medium is isotropic. However, it is straightforward to extend the calculation to anisotropic targets. In this appendix, we discuss the modifications needed to go beyond the isotropic limit.

First, the in-medium photon self-energy matrix Πλ​λ′\Pi_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}} may have nonzero off-diagonal entries, and its eigenvalues can be found by diagonalization [26]:

(Π+⁣+Π+⁣−Π+LΠ−⁣+Π−⁣−Π−LΠL+ΠL−ΠL​L)​⟶diagonalize​(Π1000Π2000Π3).\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_{++}&\Pi_{+-}&\Pi_{+L}\\ \Pi_{-+}&\Pi_{--}&\Pi_{-L}\\ \Pi_{L+}&\Pi_{L-}&\Pi_{LL}\end{pmatrix}\;\overset{\text{diagonalize}}{\longrightarrow}\;\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_{1}&0&0\\ 0&\Pi_{2}&0\\ 0&0&\Pi_{3}\end{pmatrix}\,. (120)

A DM state ϕ\phi may mix with all three photon polarizations, and Eq. (22) generalizes to

R=−ρϕρT​1ω2​Im​(Πϕ​ϕ+∑i=1,2,3Πϕ​i​Πi​ϕmϕ2−Πi),R=-\frac{\rho_{\phi}}{\rho_{T}}\,\frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\;\text{Im}\left(\Pi_{\phi\phi}+\sum_{i=1,2,3}\frac{\Pi_{\phi i}\Pi_{i\phi}}{m_{\phi}^{2}-\Pi_{i}}\right)\,, (121)

where Πϕ​i\Pi_{\phi i} is obtained from Πϕ​Aμ\Pi_{\phi A}^{\mu} by first projecting onto e±,Lμe_{\pm,L}^{\mu} and then rotating into the diagonal basis.

For vector DM ϕ\phi, the same rotation in Eq. (120) diagonalizes also the ϕ​ϕ\phi\phi and ϕ​A\phi A self-energy matrices. So each of the three polarizations of ϕ\phi mixes only with the one corresponding photon polarization, and we simply replace ΠT,L\Pi_{T,L} in Eq. (22) by Π1,2,3\Pi_{1,2,3} and average over the three polarizations to obtain the rate in the anisotropic case:

Rvector=−13κ2ρϕρTmϕ2∑i=1,2,3Im(1mϕ2−Πi).R_{\text{vector}}=-\frac{1}{3}\,\kappa^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{\phi}}{\rho_{T}}\,m_{\phi}^{2}\sum_{i=1,2,3}\text{Im}\left(\frac{1}{m_{\phi}^{2}-\Pi_{i}}\right)\,. (122)

For pseudoscalar DM, still assuming spin-degenerate electronic states, we obtain from Eq. (44):

Rpseudoscalar=−ga​e​e2​ρϕρT​14​me2​ω2​1e2​[ω2​Im​(Π+⁣++Π−⁣−)+mϕ2​Im​ΠL​L],R_{\text{pseudoscalar}}=-g_{aee}^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{\phi}}{\rho_{T}}\,\frac{1}{4m_{e}^{2}\omega^{2}}\,\frac{1}{e^{2}}\,\Bigl[\omega^{2}\,\text{Im}\,(\Pi_{++}+\Pi_{--})+m_{\phi}^{2}\,\text{Im}\,\Pi_{LL}\Bigr]\,, (123)

which generalizes Eq. (45). Note that while anisotropy allows for a nonzero mixing between the DM ϕ\phi and the photon (via its coupling to the electron’s magnetic dipole), its contribution to absorption rate is at 𝒪⁡(q2)\mathcal{O}(q^{2}) and negligible. On the other hand, if the electronic states are not spin-degenerate (e.g. due to spin-orbit coupling), one would need to explicitly compute additional matrix elements of the spin operator 𝚺\bm{\Sigma} between the spin part of the wave functions, and the absorption rate cannot be written in terms of components of the photon self-energy matrix. Also, mixing between the DM and the photon becomes relevant in this case.

For scalar DM, anisotropy may introduce mixing with all three photon polarizations, and Eq. (121) applies. The final result, however, is still expected to be dominated by the Πv¯2,v¯2\Pi_{\bar{v}^{2},\bar{v}^{2}} term from Πϕ​ϕ\Pi_{\phi\phi}, and we therefore have the same formula, Eq. (56), as in the isotropic case:

Rscalar≃−dϕ​e​e2​4​π​me2MPl2​ρϕρT​1mϕ2​Im​Πv¯2,v¯2.R_{\text{scalar}}\simeq-d_{\phi ee}^{2}\,\frac{4\pi m_{e}^{2}}{M_{\text{Pl}}^{2}}\,\frac{\rho_{\phi}}{\rho_{T}}\,\frac{1}{m_{\phi}^{2}}\,\text{Im}\,\Pi_{\bar{v}^{2},\bar{v}^{2}}\,. (124)
